procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated December 20, 1963 of the Punjab High Court in Criminal Revision No. 824 of 1963.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant contended before the High Court that the trial suffered from misjoinder of charges, that Joshi was responsible for the misappropriation, that the trial Magistrate did not produce certain documents requested by the appellant, and that this prejudiced his case. The High Court rejected these contentions and accepted the findings of the Magistrate and Additional Sessions Judge that the appellant had misappropriated the amounts, dismissing the revision.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave after the High Court dismissed his revision. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the non-production of certain documents prejudiced the appellant's case, preventing him from proving that he had handed over the misappropriated amounts to another officer.

facts: The appellant admitted to withdrawing and receiving the money in question.
He claimed that he handed the money over to another officer, Joshi, who was the designated disbursing officer.

To prove this claim, the appellant requested the production of several documents, including a memo establishing Joshi's responsibility and a remittance transfer register where he claimed to have made entries at Joshi's direction.
These documents were not produced during the trial.
Crucially, the appellant had made an extra-judicial confession to the District Inspector of Schools, admitting to having misappropriated Rs. 2,500 of the total amount.
There was also evidence that the appellant had falsely told the intended recipients that the money had already been sent to them.
law: The appellant argued that he only needed to show his case was 'reasonably probable' to cast doubt on the prosecution's evidence.
The Court considered whether the non-production of documents requested by the defense caused prejudice, preventing the accused from making their case.
application: The Supreme Court found the appellant's argument unconvincing due to his own actions and admissions.

The Court held that the appellant's extra-judicial confession to misappropriating Rs. 2,500 and his false representations to the payees made it impossible for him to raise a 'reasonable doubt' about his guilt.

In light of this confession, the Court reasoned that the requested documents were irrelevant. Even if a document showed Joshi was the official disbursing authority, it would be of 'no importance' because the appellant had already admitted to keeping the money himself.

Regarding the remittance transfer register, the Court noted two points: first, the appellant failed to object when the trial proceeded without it, and second, since the money was never actually sent to the parties, no such register or entries could logically exist.
Therefore, the Court concluded there was 'no substance' to the claim that the documents, if produced, could have helped the appellant's case or cast doubt on the prosecution's evidence.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's contention, ruling that the non-production of the documents did not prejudice his case. The Court found that the appellant's own confession of misappropriation and his false statements to payees rendered the requested documents irrelevant and made it impossible for him to establish a reasonably probable defense.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant could be convicted of the offence under s. 409 simplicitor when the charge was followed by a substantive charge of criminal breach of trust.

facts: The appellant was charged with conspiracy to commit criminal breach of trust (s. 120-B) and also faced a separate, substantive charge for criminal breach of trust (s. 409) committed in pursuance of that conspiracy.
The prosecution failed to establish the conspiracy, and the appellant was acquitted of that charge.
However, the appellant was convicted on the substantive charge of criminal breach of trust under s. 409.
law: If a charge of conspiracy to commit an offence is followed by a substantive charge for that same offence, the court can convict the accused on the substantive charge even if the prosecution fails to prove the conspiracy.
application: The Court found that the appellant was not just charged under s. 409 read with s. 120-B, but that there was a distinct and separate substantive charge under s. 409 against him.
Applying the legal principle, the failure to prove the conspiracy did not prevent the court from convicting the appellant on the separate s. 409 charge.
The Court also noted that no prejudice was caused to the appellant, as he was aware that he was facing a substantive charge under s. 409.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's contention, holding that the conviction under s. 409 simplicitor was valid because there was a substantive charge for that offence, and a conviction on that charge is permissible even if the accompanying conspiracy charge fails.

issue.issue_text: Whether the question of the appellant's duties regarding the disbursement of money could be considered by the Supreme Court when it was not raised in the High Court.

facts: The appellant's counsel argued that for a conviction under s. 409, the entrustment of money must have been in the appellant's capacity as a public servant.
The counsel contended that it was not part of the appellant's duties as a clerk to receive or disburse money, and therefore, the entrustment was not part of his official duties.
law: A legal contention that is dependent on evidence cannot be raised for the first time in the Supreme Court if it was not raised in the High Court.
application: The Supreme Court determined that the question of whether receiving and disbursing money was part of the appellant's duties was "clearly a matter of evidence."
The Court noted that this specific contention had not been raised by the appellant in the High Court.
Because the issue was dependent on evidence and was not raised in the lower court, the Court ruled that the appellant was not entitled to raise it before them.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument and refused to consider the issue, holding that since the question of his duties was a matter of evidence that was not raised in the High Court, he could not raise it for the first time before the Supreme Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant raised a reasonable doubt as to his guilt by contending that another officer was responsible for the misappropriation.

facts: The appellant admitted to receiving the moneys in question.

Evidence was presented that the appellant made an extra-judicial confession to the District Inspector of Schools, admitting he had misappropriated at least Rs. 2,500 and was prepared to deposit that amount.
There was also evidence that the appellant had falsely represented to two parties that the money owed to them had already been remitted.
The appellant contended that another officer, J, was the one responsible for the misappropriation and that he had handed the money over to J.

The appellant argued that if certain documents had been produced at trial, he could have made a 'reasonably probable case' that he gave the money to J, thereby creating a reasonable doubt about his own guilt.
application: The Supreme Court found that there was 'no question of the appellant raising any reasonable doubt' in light of the strong evidence against him.

The Court pointed specifically to three pieces of evidence that negated his claim: (a) his admission of receiving the money, (b) his confession of misappropriating a specific amount, and (c) his false representations to the parties awaiting payment.
The Court also rejected the appellant's argument regarding the non-production of documents.

It reasoned that even if the documents had shown that J was the official disbursing authority, this would not have mattered because of the appellant's own extra-judicial confession that he himself had misappropriated the funds. This confession directly undermined his claim that he had handed the money over to J.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's contention, concluding that there was 'no substance' to the argument that he could have raised a reasonable doubt. The combination of his admission to receiving the money, his confession to the misappropriation, and his false statements to creditors made it impossible to create a reasonable doubt that another officer was responsible.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the non-production of certain documents prejudiced the appellant's case, preventing him from proving that he had handed over the misappropriated amounts to another officer.
appellant_arguments: The non-production of certain documents, such as the remittance transfer register, prejudiced the appellant's case.
If the documents had been produced, the appellant could have shown that he had handed over the money to another officer, Joshi, who was the responsible disbursing officer.
The production of these documents was necessary to prove his case and to raise a reasonable doubt about the prosecution's evidence.
respondent_arguments: There was no prejudice from the non-production of documents, as a copy of one key memo was admitted in evidence, and another document was untraceable.
The request for the untraceable document was a tactic by the appellant to create confusion, knowing it did not exist.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant could be convicted of the offence under s. 409 simplicitor when the charge was followed by a substantive charge of criminal breach of trust.
appellant_arguments: The appellant could not be convicted of the offence under s. 409 simplicitor.
The trial suffered from a misjoinder of charges (specifically mentioning charges under ss. 409 and 477-A).
respondent_arguments: The appellant did not object to the charges at an earlier stage on the grounds that he would be embarrassed in his defence.
The appellant has not shown that any prejudice was caused to him by the framing of the charges.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the question of the appellant's duties regarding the disbursement of money could be considered by the Supreme Court when it was not raised in the High Court.
appellant_arguments: For a conviction under s. 409, the entrustment of money must be in the appellant's capacity as a public servant.
It was not part of the appellant's duties as a clerk to receive or disburse these moneys; he only did so at the instance of his superior, Joshi.
Therefore, the money was not entrusted to him in his capacity as a public servant.
respondent_arguments: This contention was not raised in the High Court.
The question of whether disbursing money was part of the appellant's duties is a matter of evidence.
A new argument dependent on evidence cannot be raised for the first time in the Supreme Court.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant raised a reasonable doubt as to his guilt by contending that another officer was responsible for the misappropriation.
appellant_arguments: The High Court wrongly required the appellant to prove his innocence beyond a reasonable doubt.
The appellant only needed to show that his version of events (that he handed the money to Joshi) was reasonably probable to cast doubt on the prosecution's case.
By showing his case was reasonably probable, he would be entitled to the benefit of the doubt.
respondent_arguments: There was no question of the appellant raising any reasonable doubt.
The appellant admitted to receiving the money.
The appellant confessed to the District Inspector of Schools that he had misappropriated at least Rs. 2500.
The appellant made false representations to third parties that their money had already been remitted.

cases.case_name: Willie Slaney v. The State of Madhya Pradesh
cases.principle: Used as the binding precedent to counter and reject a contrary High Court decision (Kizhakeppallik Moosa v. The State) that was relied upon by the appellant.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A matter of evidence cannot be examined by the Supreme Court if it was not raised in the High Court.
obiter: A conviction for a substantive offense is not invalidated merely because a charge of conspiracy to commit that offense fails.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the appellant's admission of having received the moneys was fatal to his defense. This admission negated any possibility of him raising a reasonable doubt as to his guilt, rendering his contentions about non-produced documents and the responsibility of another officer unsubstantial. The court also dismissed procedural challenges, finding no prejudice in the framing of the charges and refusing to entertain a new argument concerning the appellant's duties that was not raised in the lower court.
legal_tests_applied: A court can convict an accused on a substantive charge of criminal breach of trust even if the prosecution fails to establish a related charge of conspiracy.
A new argument which is a matter of evidence cannot be raised for the first time in the Supreme Court if it was not raised in the High Court.
An admission by the accused of receiving the entrusted property can be sufficient to negate the possibility of raising a reasonable doubt as to guilt.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's admission that he had received the moneys made it impossible for him to raise a reasonable doubt about his guilt.

The court found no substance in the contention that the non-production of documents prejudiced his case, as his admission of receipt undermined his claim that he could have proven he handed the money to another officer.

The argument that disbursing money was not part of his duties as a public servant was dismissed because it was a matter of evidence that was not raised in the High Court and could not be considered for the first time by the Supreme Court.
The appellant failed to show that any prejudice was caused to him by the framing of the charges, as he was aware there was a substantive charge of criminal breach of trust against him.
why_respondent_won: The prosecution's case was fundamentally supported by the appellant's own admission that he had received the moneys in question.
The respondent successfully argued that even if a conspiracy charge fails, a conviction on the substantive charge is permissible, and the appellant demonstrated no prejudice from the charges.
The respondent successfully argued that the appellant's contention regarding his official duties was a matter of evidence that could not be raised for the first time at the Supreme Court level.
